chunks.heading: The Universe Switches On
chunks.text: 1 13.8 billion years ago The Universe Switches On Every atom in your body has a very, very long backstory. Strong the big debate. Verdict: Strong. You are there Stand on the young Earth about 4.4 billion years ago and the ground is brand new. Tiny zircon crystals that will one day turn up in the Jack Hills of Western Australia are forming right now, and their chemistry hints that liquid water already pools at the surface. The Sun overhead is fainter than today's, perhaps 70 percent as bright, yet the planet is not frozen solid, a puzzle scientists still argue about. Rocks from space crash down far more often than they ever will again. The Moon, most likely born when a planet-sized body slammed into the growing Earth, hangs much closer than it does now; it has been drifting away ever since and still retreats about 3.8 centimetres a year. There is no life anyone can point to yet, no oxygen to breathe, and nobody to watch. But the ingredients are here: water, rock, energy, and carbon and oxygen cooked inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born. chunks.heading: From Slime to Dinosaurs
chunks.text: 2 4.2 billion to 66 million years ago From Slime to Dinosaurs For most of Earth's history the planet belonged to microbes, and they did a lot of the heavy lifting. Strong the big debate. Verdict: Strong. You are there It is about 508 million years ago and you are drifting over a muddy sea floor at the foot of an underwater cliff, in rocks that will one day be lifted into the Canadian Rockies. The water is busy. Trilobites plough through the mud on jointed legs. Opabinia swims past with five stalked eyes and a long flexible nozzle tipped with a grasping claw. Hallucigenia, a spiny, worm-like creature so strange that scientists first drew it upside down and back to front, picks its way across a sponge. Anomalocaris, a predator with spiny grasping limbs in front of its mouth, cruises overhead. On land there is almost nothing to see: no forests, no flowers, nothing walking on the dry ground beyond crusts of microbes. Oxygen has been building up in the air for nearly two billion years, thanks to microbes that learned to split water using sunlight. Now animals with eyes, shells and appetites are trying out every way to build a body. Soon a flow of mud will bury this scene and preserve it in astonishing detail. chunks.heading: Getting Up on Two Feet
chunks.text: 3 7 million to 400,000 years ago Getting Up on Two Feet Before big brains, fire or spears, our ancestors made one bold move: they stood up. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there About 3.66 million years ago, on the plains of what is now northern Tanzania, the volcano Sadiman has been puffing out fine ash. A light shower turns the grey powder into something like wet cement, and raindrops leave little craters in it. Every creature that crosses leaves a record. Hares hop through. Three-toed horses clip past. Guineafowl scratch about. Then come upright walkers, small by our standards, probably members of Australopithecus afarensis, the species of the famous Lucy skeleton. Their feet have an arch and a big toe in line with the others, much like yours, and their stride looks surprisingly human. Some prints are small; tracks found nearby in 2015 suggest one individual stood around 1.65 metres tall. Nobody carries a spear or wears clothes. They are simply going somewhere, across a landscape shared with grazing animals. The sun bakes the ash hard, more ash falls on top, and the walk is sealed away until Mary Leakey's team uncovers it in 1978. chunks.heading: Meet the Cousins
chunks.text: 4 1 million to 40,000 years ago Meet the Cousins For most of our story we were not alone: the world was full of other kinds of humans. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there In a limestone cave above the Anui River in Siberia's Altai Mountains, roughly 90,000 years ago, a girl of at least 13 is living her short life. No one will ever know her name; scientists will call her Denisova 11, or Denny. Her mother is a Neanderthal whose ancestors were more closely related to Neanderthals living far to the west, in Europe. Her father is a Denisovan, a member of a population so poorly known that most of what we know about it comes from DNA pulled out of bone crumbs and teeth. Her father himself carries a little Neanderthal ancestry from further back. The cave has been used on and off by both groups for a very long time. Of Denny herself, only a sliver of long bone about 2 centimetres long survives, sorted as an unremarkable scrap among thousands until a protein screen flagged it as human. Her genome is the first direct genetic evidence of a child whose parents came from two different kinds of humans. The numbers Neanderthals disappear ~41,000–39,000 years ago Radiocarbon dating across Europe suggests Neanderthal sites end in this window, with overlap with modern humans. chunks.heading: Enter Homo sapiens
chunks.text: 5 ~315,000 to 45,000 years ago Enter Homo sapiens Our species starts out in Africa, then spreads everywhere, flirting with the cousins along the way. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there On Muna, a small island off southeast Sulawesi, someone steps into the cave now called Liang Metanduno at least 67,800 years ago. They press a hand flat against the limestone wall and blow a spray of red pigment around it, probably by mouth. Then they do something clever: they adjust the outline so the fingertips look narrow and pointed, almost like claws. When the hand lifts away, a ghostly red silhouette remains. What did it mean? A signature, a ritual, a joke between friends? Nobody can say. Over tens of thousands of years, thin mineral crusts grow over the paint, and in the 2020s scientists date those crusts with uranium-series methods, which gives a minimum age for the art beneath. The artist was probably one of our own species, perhaps among the people whose relatives went on to reach Australia, though the researchers admit they cannot fully rule out another kind of human. Either way, it is one of the oldest known marks of imagination still on a cave wall. chunks.heading: Life in the Big Freeze
chunks.text: 6 ~26,500 to 14,700 years ago Life in the Big Freeze Sea levels dropped, land bridges opened, and people walked into places no human had ever seen. Strong the big debate. Verdict: Strong. You are there It is about 22,000 years ago in what is now New Mexico. Ice sheets bury most of Canada, but here in the Tularosa Basin a shallow lake spreads across the valley floor, fringed by soft, damp mud. A group of people splash along the edge. Many of the footprints they leave are small: teenagers and children, some tracks crossing and recrossing as if they were playing or running errands. The same basin's mud also holds tracks of mammoths and giant ground sloths, animals that still roam North America. Seeds of a water plant called ditchgrass sink into the shallows, and pollen from conifers drifts down from the hills. Thousands of years later, those seeds, that pollen, grains of quartz and ancient lake mud will each be dated by independent teams and methods, and they keep landing between roughly 21,000 and 23,000 years ago. If those dates hold, these kids were walking in the Americas thousands of years before most textbooks said anyone had arrived. chunks.heading: The Great Melt
chunks.text: 7 14,700 to 8,000 years ago The Great Melt The ice cracked, the seas rose, and the climate lurched like a car with a learner driver. No receipts yet the big debate. Verdict: No receipts yet. You are there Somewhere on the coast of what is now South Australia, generation after generation, the sea is coming closer. As the world's great ice sheets melt, ocean levels climb: on average about a metre a century, and faster during meltwater pulses. Grandparents point to places where they once walked dry-footed that are now under water. Hunting grounds turn into shallows, then open sea. Hills become islands. People adjust: they move camps, rename places, and above all they tell each other what happened. Thousands of years later, Aboriginal stories recorded by outsiders in the 19th and 20th centuries describe a time when the coastline lay far out, when islands were joined to the mainland, and when the sea rose and drowned the land. Geographer Patrick Nunn and linguist Nicholas Reid argue that some of these stories may preserve real memories of shorelines that vanished more than 7,000 years ago. If they are right, these are among the oldest surviving accounts passed down by word of mouth anywhere on Earth. chunks.heading: Monuments Before Farms
chunks.text: 8 ~11,600 to 10,000 years ago Monuments Before Farms People carved giant stone pillars before they had fully become farmers, which flipped an old textbook story on its head. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain in what is now southeastern Türkiye, around 11,000 years ago, people are cutting a pillar out of the bedrock. They have no metal tools and no domesticated animals to haul loads, only stone, rope, wood and muscle. When a T-shaped pillar is finished, carvers bring it to life with foxes, boars, snakes, cranes and vultures. On some pillars, arms and hands wrap around the sides above a belt and a fox-pelt loincloth, as if the stone were a stylised person. Nearby, grinding slabs turn wild cereals into mash or dough. Bones of wild gazelle and aurochs pile up, perhaps from large gatherings. Out in the quarry, an unfinished pillar about 7 metres long still lies in the rock, abandoned, possibly after it cracked. Nobody here is a farmer in the full sense yet. That is exactly why archaeologists are still arguing about what this place was for. chunks.heading: Farming Changes Everything
chunks.text: 9 ~12,000 to 8,000 years ago Farming Changes Everything Humans tamed wheat, rice, maize, goats and cattle, and in return, farming tamed us. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there It is around 7000 BCE on the Konya Plain in central Anatolia, and there are no streets. Çatalhöyük is a honeycomb of mud-brick houses packed wall to wall, and you get home by walking across the rooftops and climbing down a ladder through a hole that also lets the smoke from the oven out. Inside, the walls are plastered white and sometimes painted; horns of wild cattle are set into benches and walls. Some of the dead lie beneath the platforms where the living sleep. Families grow wheat, barley, peas and lentils, herd sheep and goats, and still hunt wild animals. Ancient DNA from more than a hundred people buried here hints at a surprise: relatives buried beneath the same houses were often linked through their mothers' lines, and females tended to receive more grave goods. Life is crowded and busy, and in some ways harder than foraging; skeletons show rising tooth decay and head injuries. Still, people keep living here for well over a thousand years. The numbers Independent farming inventions at least 11 regions Plants and animals were domesticated separately in places including the Fertile Crescent, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica and the Andes. chunks.heading: Cities and the First Writing
chunks.text: 10 ~5,500 to 3,900 years ago Cities and the First Writing Writing was not invented for poetry. It was invented because somebody needed to count the barley. No receipts yet the big debate. Verdict: No receipts yet. You are there Uruk, southern Mesopotamia, around 3200 BCE. The city is enormous for its time, with perhaps tens of thousands of people, temple precincts decorated with mosaics of coloured clay cones, and canals branching off from the Euphrates. In a storeroom, an administrator wets a lump of clay, flattens it into a tablet and presses a reed stylus into it: a sign for barley, round and crescent-shaped marks for quantities, a sign group that might be a person's name or a job title. This is not literature. Most of the earliest tablets are bookkeeping: rations, livestock, workers, beer. One often-quoted tablet tallies barley over 37 months and carries a sign group read as Kushim, which might be the earliest recorded name of a person, or might simply be an office. Nobody here thinks they are inventing history. They are trying not to lose track of the grain. Within a few centuries, scribes will be writing hymns, laws and stories. chunks.heading: The Age of Pyramids
chunks.text: 11 ~4,700 to 4,000 years ago The Age of Pyramids Giant tombs, giant stones hauled across Britain, and a drought that may or may not have toppled kings. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there Around 2560 BCE, an inspector named Merer is keeping a logbook on papyrus. He leads a team of roughly 40 men, and they work the Nile by boat. Their job: collect blocks of fine white limestone at the quarries of Tura, across the river, and ferry them to Giza, where King Khufu's pyramid is rising. The diary notes, day by day, where the crew sleeps and when they sail, and it mentions a basin called the Lake of Khufu near the building site, reachable by boat when the water is high. Merer's crew are not the whip-driven masses of old films; they are organised, supplied and recorded, part of a state machine able to move millions of tonnes of stone. About 4,500 years later, in 2013, fragments of Merer's diary turn up at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, a harbour where his team later worked. They are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found, and they give us the building of the Great Pyramid in the words of someone who was there. chunks.heading: The First Global Economy Crashes
chunks.text: 12 ~3,700 to 3,100 years ago The First Global Economy Crashes Copper from Cyprus, tin from far inland, amber from the Baltic: then the whole network fell apart. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there It is about 1300 BCE off the rocky cape of Uluburun in southwestern Türkiye, and a merchant ship is in trouble. She is roughly 15 metres long, built of cedar, and she is carrying the Bronze Age in her hold: about ten tonnes of copper in 354 flat 'oxhide' ingots, roughly a tonne of tin to turn it into bronze, some 175 ingots of blue and turquoise glass, logs of African blackwood, hippo and elephant ivory, amber probably from the Baltic, jars of terebinth resin, and a gold scarab bearing the name of Egypt's Queen Nefertiti. The cargo comes from lands stretching from Egypt and Canaan to Cyprus, Mycenaean Greece and beyond. The ship goes down in about 45 metres of water. In 1982 a young sponge diver describes seeing 'metal biscuits with ears' on the sea floor, and archaeologists spend eleven summers bringing her story back up. chunks.heading: The Age of Big Questions
chunks.text: 13 800 to 200 BCE The Age of Big Questions Across Eurasia, people started asking what a good life is, and they also invented pocket change. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there Sardis, capital of Lydia in western Anatolia, a little before 600 BCE. Grains of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, wash down the Pactolus stream, and Lydian craftsmen have learned to turn them into something new: small lumps of standard weight, struck with a punch and stamped with a lion's head. A trader no longer has to weigh metal at every deal. He can count. Within a few generations Lydian refiners are separating pure gold from pure silver, and the idea of the coin spreads through the Greek world, while China and India develop metal money of their own. In these same centuries, from Greek cities and Persian lands to the Ganges plain, the hills of Judah and the rival states of China, teachers and writers are asking restless questions about justice, suffering, duty and how to live. Did coins, cities and busy markets help make room for these new ideas? Historians are still arguing. The numbers 'Axial Age' 800–200 BCE Philosopher Karl Jaspers coined the term in 1949 for a burst of new thought across Eurasia. chunks.heading: Empires and Long Roads
chunks.text: 14 ~550 BCE to 220 CE Empires and Long Roads Persia, Rome, the Mauryas and the Han built roads so good that ideas, silk and germs could travel them too. No receipts yet the big debate. Verdict: No receipts yet. You are there In 126 BCE a battered traveller rides back into the Han capital, Chang'an. His name is Zhang Qian, and about thirteen years earlier he set out with roughly a hundred companions on a mission for Emperor Wu: find the Yuezhi people in the far west and recruit them against the Xiongnu. It went badly. The Xiongnu captured him and held him for about ten years; he married there and had a son. He escaped, reached the Yuezhi, failed to persuade them, was captured again, and escaped again. Of the original party, only he and one companion make it home. But Zhang Qian brings back something more valuable than an alliance: reports of Ferghana and its magnificent horses, of Bactria's markets where he saw cloth and bamboo from southwest China that had come by way of India, and of Parthia and lands beyond. The court listens. Within decades Han envoys and caravans are heading west, and the web of routes later nicknamed the Silk Road is humming. chunks.heading: Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun
chunks.text: 15 ~300 to 950 CE Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun New faiths spread across continents while volcanoes, plague and drought tested every empire. Hot debate the big debate. Verdict: Hot debate. You are there Constantinople, 536 CE. The historian Procopius notices something eerie and writes it down: for the whole year, he says, the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon. Far to the west, Irish annals will record a 'failure of bread'. Ice cores show why: a large volcanic eruption that year filled the northern sky with sulphate haze, and another followed around 540. Tree rings across the Northern Hemisphere record some of the coldest summers of the last two thousand years. Then, in 541, a new terror arrives by ship at Pelusium in Egypt: plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It reaches Constantinople the next year. Procopius, still writing, claims that at the peak ten thousand people a day are dying in the city. Historians argue over that number and over how deadly the pandemic was across the whole Mediterranean. They agree it was a frightening time to be alive, and that the people living through it had no idea the two disasters were linked to faraway volcanoes and fleas. The numbers 536 CE eruption eruptions in 536 and ~540 Ice cores reveal two eruptions that caused one of the sharpest Northern Hemisphere coolings of the last two millennia. chunks.heading: The World Joins Up
chunks.text: 16 ~900 to 1500 CE The World Joins Up Norse ships, Polynesian canoes, camel caravans and Chinese paper money: the planet was getting connected. No receipts yet the big debate. Verdict: No receipts yet. You are there The northern tip of Newfoundland, the year 1021. Norse voyagers from Greenland have built turf halls around timber frames near a shallow bay, and today someone is cutting wood with an iron blade, leaving clean, flat cuts that no stone tool would make. They have no idea the wood carries a hidden timestamp. In 993 a burst of cosmic radiation, most likely from a storm on the Sun, left a spike of radiocarbon in every tree growing that year. A thousand years later, scientists count the rings outward from that spike to the bark edge on three pieces of wood from three different trees, and each one was felled in 1021. The Norse do not stay long; the sagas describe voyages to a land called Vinland and tense meetings with the people already living there. But for a moment, as far as we know, human journeys have looped all the way around the planet: travellers who came west across the Atlantic meet the descendants of people who came east into the Americas from Asia. chunks.heading: Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not.
chunks.text: Flood · Primeval age (setting); texts c. 1700 BCE onward Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not. Mesopotamian, Hebrew Bible, Greek, Hindu Busted. Verdict: Busted. The account. Atrahasis; Epic of Gilgamesh Tablet XI; Genesis 6-9; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1; Deucalion in Apollodorus. Written: Atrahasis c. 1700 BCE; Genesis flood strands probably 1st millennium BCE; Shatapatha Brahmana c. 800-500 BCE A divine decision to wipe the world clean, one favoured man warned in advance, a boat stocked with living things, and a landing on a mountain. The Babylonian Utnapishtim sends out birds; Noah does the same; the Hindu Manu is towed to safety by a fish that grows enormous; the Greek Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulate the Earth by throwing stones over their shoulders. The shared skeleton is striking, and the Mesopotamian versions are the oldest written ones. The flood then swept away all these creatures, and Manu alone remained here. The evidence Greenland ice cores preserve unbroken annual layers counted back some 60,000 years; a planet-wide sea over the ice sheet would have left a break that is not there. chunks.heading: Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote
chunks.text: Lost city · c. 9600 BCE (setting); told c. 360 BCE Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote Greek Busted. Verdict: Busted. The account. Plato, Timaeus 24e-25d and Critias. chunks.heading: The Laetoli footprint makers
chunks.text: The first walkers whose actual steps we can follow The Laetoli footprint makers A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there. about 3.66 million years ago Laetoli, Ngorongoro district, Tanzania. In 1976, at Laetoli in northern Tanzania, a playful fight with dried elephant dung sent the researcher Andrew Hill diving to the ground, where he noticed animal tracks pressed into hardened ash. The search that followed, led by Mary Leakey, uncovered in 1978 what she had hoped for: a trail of about 70 hominin footprints stretching some 24 metres at Site G. They were made about 3.66 million years ago, after ash from a nearby eruption was dampened by light rain and then set almost like cement. At least two walkers left the trail, and a third probably stepped into the prints of one of them. Heel strikes, raised arches and big toes in line with the other toes show upright striding. The story keeps growing. In 2015 a new trail at Site S revealed an individual nicknamed S1 who may have stood about 165 cm, much taller than Lucy, hinting at large size differences within the species. In 2019 a team re-excavated odd tracks at Site A, first uncovered in 1976 and once blamed on a bear. They concluded a hominin made them, walking with a cross-over step, which suggests more than one kind of biped shared this landscape. What we actually have Hominin trackways in the Footprint Tuff at Laetoli Sites G, S and A, plus casts, photographs and 3D scans. How we know Radiometric dating of the volcanic tuffs; footprint shape compared with humans, other primates and bears; stature estimated from footprint length. The Site G trail was reburied in 1979 and re-protected in the 1990s after tree roots began damaging the prints.

chunks.heading: Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh
chunks.text: Celebrity fossil who never asked to be the 'missing link' Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong. about 3.2 million years ago Hadar, Afar region, Ethiopia. On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray spotted a piece of arm bone in a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia. Over the following weeks the team recovered several hundred bone fragments from one individual, about 40 percent of a skeleton. That night the camp played the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' over and over, and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh, 'you are marvelous'. She stood about 1.1 metres tall, weighed perhaps 29 kg, and walked upright, while keeping long, strong arms useful for climbing. Now, what she was not. She was not the 'missing link': human evolution is a branching bush, not a chain. She was not the oldest hominin; older ones, such as Ardipithecus, are known. She was probably not alone: other hominin species likely shared the region at around the same time. And her death is an open case. A 2016 CT study argued that her unhealed fractures fit a fall from a tall tree; critics answer that many breaks could have formed long after death, as the bones fossilized and eroded. In 2025 she left Ethiopia for her first European exhibition, in Prague. What we actually have Several hundred fragments of a single skeleton (about 40 percent complete), held at the National Museum of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa. How we know Radiometric dating of volcanic layers bracketing the find; comparative anatomy of pelvis, knee and ankle for upright walking; high-resolution CT scanning (2008) of the bones for injury analysis. chunks.heading: The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy')
chunks.text: Homo erectus kid with a sore back and a bad tooth The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy') The icon of early human long-distance walking was a child, probably with a toothache. about 1.5 million years ago Nariokotome, West Turkana, Kenya. In August 1984 Kamoya Kimeu, the celebrated fossil finder of the National Museums of Kenya, spotted a small piece of skull on a slope near the Nariokotome River, west of Lake Turkana. Excavations led by Richard Leakey and Alan Walker grew it into the most complete early human skeleton then known: about 1.5 million years old and assigned to Homo erectus (some call it Homo ergaster). He was young. His teeth were still coming in, and studies of tooth growth lines suggest he was probably around 8 years old, although estimates have ranged from about 7 to 12, because his species likely grew up faster than we do. He was already tall for his age, long-legged and narrow-hipped, a body plan suited to walking in heat. Early estimates had him becoming a 180 cm giant; later work suggests a more modest adult height. His lower jaw shows signs of infection, and a 2013 re-study argued that his spine reflects a herniated disc rather than a growth disorder, as had once been proposed. So one of the best-known fossils of our lineage is probably best imagined as a lanky, sore-backed kid with a bad tooth. What we actually have A nearly complete skeleton, including skull, jaw, spine, ribs, pelvis and limb bones. How we know Dental development and tooth microstructure for age; skeletal proportions for body size; comparative anatomy and pathology studies of the spine and jaw. A fossil primate, Kamoyapithecus, is named in honour of Kamoya Kimeu, the man who found the boy.

chunks.heading: Denny (Denisova 11)
chunks.text: Daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father Denny (Denisova 11) A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups. about 90,000 years ago Denisova Cave, Altai Mountains, Russia. Denisova Cave in Siberia has produced thousands of bone scraps too broken to identify by eye. Researchers screened them with ZooMS, a method that fingerprints the collagen protein in bone, and in 2016 reported that one splinter, among roughly 2,000 fragments, came from a hominin rather than a mammoth or a bear. It was only about 2.5 cm long. Its genome, published in 2018, told one of the most surprising family stories in science. This individual, a girl at least 13 years old, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father: not distant mixed ancestry, but first-generation parents from two different groups. Her father's own genome carried traces of an earlier Neanderthal ancestor, so meetings like this had happened before. Her mother was genetically closer to Neanderthals who lived later in Croatia than to an earlier Neanderthal from the same Siberian cave, which hints that Neanderthal populations moved across Eurasia. Denny lived roughly 90,000 years ago. We have no face, no grave and no tools linked to her; just a sliver of long bone that changed estimates of how often these groups met and had children. What we actually have A single fragment of long bone (specimen DC1227), about 2.5 cm long. How we know ZooMS collagen fingerprinting to spot the fragment; ancient DNA sequencing, including patterns of heterozygosity showing one Neanderthal and one Denisovan parent; bone cortex thickness for minimum age. Only a handful of Denisovan fossils have ever been identified, so a large part of what we know about the group comes from DNA

chunks.heading: Shanidar Z
chunks.text: Neanderthal woman rebuilt from 200 fragments Shanidar Z Her skull had been flattened to about 2 cm thick; scientists put her face back together piece by piece. about 75,000 years ago Shanidar Cave, Iraqi Kurdistan, Iraq. In 2018, working at Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan for the first time in about half a century, a team led by Cambridge researchers found the upper body of a Neanderthal. Her skull had been crushed in the ground to roughly 2 cm thick. Conservator Lucia Lopez-Polin strengthened the fragile pieces on site, and in the lab more than 200 fragments were reassembled, a high-stakes 3D jigsaw. Proteins in her tooth enamel point to a female; heavy wear, with front teeth ground down to the roots, suggests she died in her mid-40s, about 75,000 years ago. She stood roughly 150 cm tall and had some of the smallest adult arm bones in the Neanderthal record. She lay on her side with her left hand under her head, with a rock behind the head, within a cluster of burials beside a tall vertical rock. She lies close to Shanidar 4, the famous 'flower burial' reported in the 1960s. A 2023 study argues that the pollen there was most likely carried in by burrowing bees rather than left by mourners. The flowers may be gone, but the pattern of repeated burial at one spot still suggests these Neanderthals returned to, and remembered, their dead. What we actually have A crushed skull and upper skeleton excavated in 2018, reconstructed from more than 200 fragments. How we know Enamel peptide analysis for sex; dental wear for age; stratigraphy and luminescence dating of the cave deposits; palynology and bee-burrow analysis for the pollen question. Her face was modelled by the palaeoartists Adrie and Alfons Kennis for the 2024 documentary Secrets of the Neanderthals.

chunks.heading: Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1)
chunks.text: Woman at the centre of one of the oldest known cremations Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1) Forty thousand years ago, on the shore of a lake that no longer exists, people cremated a young woman with care. about 40,000 years ago Lake Mungo, Willandra Lakes, New South Wales, Australia. In July 1968 the geologist Jim Bowler was mapping ancient shorelines in the dry Willandra Lakes of New South Wales when he noticed burnt bone weathering out of a sand dune at Lake Mungo. The remains were of a young woman. Her body had been burned, the bones broken, and then burned again before being placed in a small pit: one of the oldest known cremations anywhere. In 1974, nearby, Bowler found a man buried on his back with his hands clasped, his body sprinkled with red ochre. Dating arguments ran for decades, with estimates from under 30,000 to over 60,000 years. A 2003 multi-method study placed both burials at about 40,000 years old, which makes these among the oldest funeral rituals known for modern humans. Her story also belongs to the present. Mungo Lady was returned to her Traditional Owners, the Paakantyi, Mutthi Mutthi and Ngiyampaa peoples, in 1992; Mungo Man was returned in 2015 and brought home to Lake Mungo in 2017. For these communities she is an ancestor, not a specimen, and her return reshaped how Australian science works with Aboriginal people and their dead. What we actually have Burnt and fragmented skeletal remains from a small pit in the Mungo lunette, plus the nearby ochre burial of Mungo Man. How we know Optically stimulated luminescence and other dating of the dune layers; osteology of burnt bone; burial context. Lake Mungo has been dry for thousands of years; the burials sit in a crescent dune, the 'Walls of China', that formed along its old shore.

chunks.heading: The children of the Ice Age caves
chunks.text: Toddlers who drew on ceilings and teenagers who fetched clay The children of the Ice Age caves Some of the marks in France's painted caves were made by toddlers, probably held up by an adult to reach the ceiling. about 17,000 to 13,000 years ago Rouffignac, Tuc d'Audoubert and Niaux caves, France. In Rouffignac Cave in the Dordogne, probably around 13,000 years ago, people dragged soft fingers through the clay of a chamber ceiling, leaving looping lines called flutings. Kevin Sharpe and Leslie Van Gelder measured the width of three-finger marks and compared them with flutings made by modern volunteers. They concluded that some ceiling marks were made by children about 2 to 5 years old. Given the height of the ceiling, the smallest artists were probably lifted by adults. Picture an Ice Age grown-up holding a toddler up so the child could add their own lines. Footprints tell related stories. In 2013 three expert San trackers from Namibia, invited by the Tracking in Caves project, read Ice Age prints in caves of the French Pyrenees. At Tuc d'Audoubert they identified a man of about 38 and a boy of about 14 walking on their heels near a clay pit, probably gathering clay for the famous modelled bison about 15 metres away. At Niaux they read one set of prints as those of a girl of about 12, although those prints are not securely dated. Children were not just tagging along; they were probably taking part. How we know Metric comparison of finger-mark widths with experimental flutings; expert Indigenous tracking combined with archaeological recording of footprints.
