chunks.text: Teenager who helped link the first Americans to living Native peoples Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48) A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats. about 13,000 to 12,000 years ago Hoyo Negro, Sac Actun cave system, Quintana Roo, Mexico. Around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, on the Yucatan Peninsula, a teenage girl walked through a dry cave system in the dark, probably searching for water. She fell into a deep pit now called Hoyo Negro, 'black hole'. Later, as the Ice Age ended and sea levels rose, the caves flooded. In 2007 cave divers exploring the drowned passages found her skeleton on the pit floor alongside the bones of saber-toothed cats, giant ground sloths and other animals that had made the same fatal mistake. Researchers named her Naia, after water nymphs. She was about 15 or 16. Her mitochondrial DNA belongs to a lineage (D1) found among living Native Americans, while her skull has the long, narrow shape typical of early Paleoamericans. Together these support the idea that the first Americans and today's Indigenous peoples share ancestry despite differences in appearance. Later analyses, presented at a 2017 conference, suggest she was small and slender, went through repeated periods of hunger, and may have given birth before she died. Hers was likely a hard and mobile life, cut short by a single misstep in the dark. What we actually have A nearly complete skeleton recovered from an underwater pit, with associated Ice Age animal bones. How we know Radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating of tooth enamel and cave mineral deposits; mitochondrial DNA; skeletal and dental analysis. Her remains lay underwater for thousands of years; mineral crusts on the bones helped scientists date her.

chunks.heading: Otzi the Iceman
chunks.text: Copper Age traveller, murder victim and the most studied body on Earth Otzi the Iceman Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder. about 5,300 years ago (c. 3350 to 3100 BCE) Tisenjoch, Otztal Alps, South Tyrol, Italy (near the Austrian border). On 19 September 1991, hikers Erika and Helmut Simon saw a brown body emerging from melting ice high in the Otztal Alps and assumed he was an unlucky modern climber. He had died about 5,300 years ago. Surveyors later placed the spot 92.56 metres inside Italy, which is why he now rests in a museum in Bolzano. For a decade he seemed to have died of exposure; then, in 2001, X-rays revealed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. He also had a head injury. His stomach, analysed in 2018, held a last meal eaten between half an hour and two hours before death: very fatty ibex meat, red deer, einkorn wheat and traces of bracken. The copper of his axe came from southern Tuscany. His 61 tattoos, a 2024 experimental study argues, were most likely hand-poked rather than cut. And a 2023 genome re-analysis changed his look: he probably had dark skin, dark eyes and male-pattern baldness, and more than 90 percent of his ancestry came from early farmers with roots in Anatolia. The pale, shaggy Iceman of older museum reconstructions reflected modern assumptions more than his DNA. What we actually have A naturally mummified body with clothing, a copper axe, a bow, arrows, a dagger and other gear. How we know Radiocarbon dating; X-ray and CT imaging; stomach-content analysis (proteomics, lipids, DNA, microscopy); lead-isotope sourcing of the axe; whole-genome sequencing. After a long legal dispute, the couple who found him were awarded a finder's fee of 150,000 euro

chunks.heading: Kushim
chunks.text: Possibly the first named person in history, and possibly an accountant Kushim The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt. about 3200 to 3000 BCE Uruk, southern Iraq. Around 3200 to 3000 BCE, in the city of Uruk in what is now southern Iraq, administrators pressed signs into small clay tablets. The earliest writing, called proto-cuneiform, was not yet used for letters or poems; it was bookkeeping. One tablet, now in the Schoyen Collection, records a large total of barley over 37 months and ends with two signs read KU and SHIM. The same combination appears on about 18 tablets. Yuval Noah Harari's bestseller Sapiens made the reading famous, rendering it as 29,086 measures of barley, signed Kushim. Specialists are more cautious. The signs could be a personal name, but they could also be a job title or the name of an office, because the earliest script rarely made the difference clear. The texts linked to Kushim deal with barley and grain products, probably connected with the malting and brewing work of a large institution. If Kushim was a person, then the first name we can read belongs not to a king but to someone checking that the numbers added up. That is a rather reassuring start for written history. What we actually have Proto-cuneiform clay tablets from Uruk (for example MS 1717 in the Schoyen Collection) bearing the sign sequence KU.SHIM. How we know Decipherment of proto-cuneiform numerical systems and administrative formats, comparing sign use across hundreds of archaic tablets. A rival for the 'oldest known name', Gal-Sal, appears on a tablet from around 3100 BCE together with two enslaved people, En-pap X and Sukkalgir.

chunks.heading: Merer, inspector of boatmen
chunks.text: Middle manager whose logbook tracks work on the Great Pyramid Merer, inspector of boatmen The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid. about 2560 BCE (reign of Khufu, year 27) Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt (logbook found at Wadi al-Jarf, Red Sea coast). In 2013, at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on Egypt's Red Sea coast, a team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard found papyrus rolls left at the entrance of storage galleries cut into the rock. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known, from late in the reign of King Khufu, around 2560 BCE. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer, who led a crew of about 40 boatmen. His entries are laid out day by day in neat columns, recording a steady rhythm: loading limestone at the Tura quarries across the Nile, sailing to Akhet-Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the ancient name for the Great Pyramid site at Giza, stopping overnight at places such as the She-Khufu basin, and heading back for more. The fine Tura limestone was probably destined for the pyramid's outer casing. Merer also mentions Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, as the official in charge of a harbour at Giza. No pharaoh speaks in these pages, and there are no secret machines; just a supervisor counting trips and days. It is the closest thing we have to a worker's view of the Great Pyramid in its final years of construction. What we actually have Fragments of papyrus logbooks (the 'Diary of Merer') found at Wadi al-Jarf, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo. How we know Hieratic palaeography and translation; regnal-year dating in the texts; excavation of the Wadi al-Jarf harbour and storage galleries. The papyri probably ended up at the Red Sea because Merer's crew

chunks.heading: Puabi of Ur
chunks.text: Queen or high lady buried in gold, and not alone Puabi of Ur Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story. about 2600 to 2500 BCE Royal Cemetery, Ur, southern Iraq. In the late 1920s, Leonard Woolley's excavators at Ur opened a tomb numbered PG 800 and found a woman on a wooden bier, her upper body covered in beads of gold, silver, lapis lazuli and carnelian, with a spectacular headdress of gold leaves, ribbons and flowers. A lapis cylinder seal nearby named her Puabi, with the title nin, meaning 'queen' or 'lady'. Unusually, the seal names no husband, which likely signals that her rank stood on its own. She died around 2600 to 2500 BCE, probably at about 40 years old. She was not buried alone. Woolley recorded dozens of attendants in her burial complex, about 52 by one count, and imagined them calmly drinking poison. In 2011, CT scans of two skulls from other graves in the Royal Cemetery suggested a harsher end: blunt-force wounds, probably from a pointed, weighted weapon, plus signs of heating and traces of mercury sulphide, possibly used to slow decay while the bodies were laid out. Behind the glitter of the headdress sits a sobering question: what did royal display cost the people around it? What we actually have Tomb PG 800 with Puabi's skeleton, jewellery, headdress and inscribed cylinder seals, now largely at the Penn Museum, Philadelphia. How we know Excavation records; reading of the cuneiform seal inscription; later CT scanning and forensic analysis of skulls from the Royal Cemetery. Her name is Akkadian, not Sumerian, and may mean something like 'word of my father'.

chunks.heading: Enheduanna
chunks.text: Princess, high priestess and the first named author Enheduanna The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile. about 2300 to 2250 BCE Ur, southern Iraq. Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad built the first great empire of Mesopotamia and installed his daughter as en-priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She took, or was given, the name Enheduanna. In the 1920s Leonard Woolley's team at Ur found a calcite disk showing her at a ritual in a flounced robe, with an inscription naming her as Sargon's daughter. Her fame rests on poetry. Several Sumerian hymns, copied by scribes centuries later, name her as their author, which would make her the first named author in world literature. In the poem known as 'The Exaltation of Inana' she speaks in the first person: pushed out of her office during a revolt, she describes her exile with raw emotion and pleads with the goddess Inana to restore her. It is vivid, personal and startlingly angry. Scholars debate how much she composed herself, because the surviving copies are around 500 years younger than she is, and the attribution may partly reflect later tradition. Either way, Mesopotamian scribes chose to remember a woman as the voice behind some of their greatest hymns. I, En-hedu-ana the en priestess, entered my holy jipar in your service. The Exaltation of Inana (Inana B), ETCSL translation, University of Oxford What we actually have An inscribed calcite (alabaster) disk from Ur (Penn Museum) naming her; Old Babylonian clay-tablet copies of hymns attributed to her; seals of her servants. How we know Excavation at Ur; reading of Sumerian and Akkadian inscriptions; philology of the hymn manuscripts and their colophons. The disk showing her had been smashed in antiquity;

chunks.heading: Hammurabi of Babylon
chunks.text: King who carved his idea of justice into stone Hammurabi of Babylon His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country. reigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE Babylon, central Iraq (stele found at Susa, Iran). Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE and turned a mid-sized city-state into the leading power of Mesopotamia. Late in his reign he set up a tall black stone stele, over 2 metres high, topped by a carving of the king standing before a god usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and guardian of justice. Below it: a prologue, about 282 laws, and an epilogue inviting anyone wronged to come and have the inscription read to them. The laws are not an even-handed modern code. Penalties depend on social status: destroying the eye of a free man could cost an eye, while injuring a commoner or an enslaved person meant a payment. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed the owner could be put to death. Many scholars now read the collection less as a rulebook judges followed and more as a royal showcase of wise judgments. The stele had its own adventures: an Elamite king carried it to Susa as war booty in the 12th century BCE, and French excavators found it there in 1901 and 1902. Today it stands in the Louvre, still making its case to visitors. to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak Prologue to the Laws of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King (1910) What we actually have The basalt stele in the Louvre, fragments of other copies, and later clay-tablet copies of the laws, plus Hammurabi's surviving letters. How we know Decipherment of Akkadian cuneiform; comparison with legal documents, contracts and r

chunks.heading: Ea-nasir and Nanni
chunks.text: Copper merchant with a bad reputation, and his furious customer Ea-nasir and Nanni The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at. about 1750 BCE Ur, southern Iraq. Around 1750 BCE, a man named Nanni in the city of Ur was fed up. He had dealt with Ea-nasir, a merchant who brought copper up the Gulf through Dilmun (modern Bahrain), and received ingots he considered below the agreed quality. Worse, he said his servant had been treated rudely and his money had not come back. So he had a clay tablet written, and it survives: a small letter about 11.6 cm tall, now in the British Museum. He complains that messengers he sent to collect his money came back empty-handed, several times, even through dangerous territory, and he demands to be treated with respect. The best twist: the tablet was found in Ea-nasir's own house at Ur during Leonard Woolley's excavations, alongside other letters grumbling about copper deliveries. Either Ea-nasir kept his complaints on file, or complaints were simply a large share of his business correspondence. Nearly 4,000 years later he has become an internet legend, a sort of patron saint of bad suppliers. The tablet is also a serious window onto long-distance metal trade, credit and business etiquette in the Old Babylonian world. What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt? Nanni to Ea-nasir, UET V 81, trans. A. Leo Oppenheim, Letters from Mesopotamia (1967) What we actually have Clay tablet BM 131236 (UET V 81), written in Akkadian cuneiform, plus other letters from the same house at Ur. How we know Excavation context at Ur; decipherment and translation of Old Babylonian Akkadian letters. Guinness World Records lists the tablet as the oldest written customer complaint.

chunks.heading: Hatshepsut
chunks.text: Queen who made herself king Hatshepsut She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told. reigned about 1479 to 1458 BCE Thebes (Deir el-Bahri), Luxor, Egypt. Hatshepsut was the daughter of one pharaoh, the wife of another, and regent for a third, the young Thutmose III. Then she did something unusual: she had herself crowned king. For about two decades she ruled with full royal titles and was often shown with a king's kilt and false beard. Her projects include the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri, whose reliefs celebrate an expedition to the distant land of Punt that returned with incense trees and exotic animals. After her death her images were broken and her name cut from monuments, long read as Thutmose III's revenge. A 2025 study of 1920s excavation archives suggests a cooler motive. Many statues were broken at weak points such as the neck, waist and knees in ways consistent with ritual 'deactivation', some faces were left intact, and the pieces were reused as building material. The erasure also came years into Thutmose's sole reign, which fits succession politics better than personal hatred. Even her body is debated: a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers in 2007 on the basis of a tooth, but that match has not been confirmed by DNA and some scholars remain unconvinced. What we actually have Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, obelisks at Karnak, hundreds of statue fragments, inscriptions, and a debated mummy (KV60-A). How we know Hieroglyphic inscriptions; archaeology of statue deposits and archival excavation records; CT imaging and dental comparison for the mummy. Isotope analysis of mummified baboons, animals Egyptians imported from Punt, points to a source region aro

chunks.heading: Tutankhamun
chunks.text: Teenage king whose body tells a story of illness Tutankhamun Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane. died about 1323 BCE Valley of the Kings (tomb KV62), Luxor, Egypt. Howard Carter's 1922 discovery of a nearly intact royal tomb made Tutankhamun the world's most famous pharaoh, although he was a minor king who died young, around 1323 BCE. What does his body tell us? A 2010 study combining CT scans and DNA from royal mummies concluded that he died at about 19 and that his parents were probably brother and sister: the mummy from tomb KV55, most likely Akhenaten, and an unnamed woman known as the 'Younger Lady' from tomb KV35. The study reported a clubfoot, bone death in part of his left foot (Kohler disease II), a cleft palate, and DNA from the most dangerous malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. It proposed malaria combined with the bone disease as the most likely cause of death. His tomb held about 130 walking sticks and staves, some with signs of use, which fits a king who probably walked with pain. Treat the details with care: other researchers have questioned the ancient DNA methods and some diagnoses, and a broken leg remains debated as either injury or damage from embalming or excavation. The golden mask covered a young man who was probably often unwell. What we actually have His mummy, CT data, DNA samples, and the contents of tomb KV62, including about 130 sticks and staves. How we know CT scanning, ancient DNA (Y-chromosome and autosomal markers) for kinship, pathogen DNA testing, and study of the tomb objects. Two mummified foetuses buried in his tomb may have been his daughters, according to the same 2010 DNA study.

chunks.heading: The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht)
chunks.text: Royal tomb workers who staged the first recorded strike The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht) When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out. about 1157 BCE (year 29 of Ramesses III) Deir el-Medina, west bank of Luxor, Egypt. The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, and were paid in rations of grain. In year 29 of Ramesses III, around 1157 BCE, those rations were badly overdue. So the crew did something no earlier record shows: they stopped work and walked out. The scribe Amennakht kept notes, which survive on a papyrus now in Turin. The workers marched past the guard posts of the necropolis, sat down behind temples on the west bank, and refused to go back, insisting their grievance be reported to Pharaoh. Officials delivered rations; the crew returned; supplies slipped again; they struck again. The dispute stretched over several months. For the officials it was an embarrassment. For historians it is priceless: a record of ordinary workers in a powerful state organizing, negotiating and getting at least part of what they were owed. The village was unusually literate, and its rubbish heaps have yielded thousands of inscribed potsherds and limestone flakes, including a register of work absences whose excuses range from illness to brewing beer. On this day the crew passed the five guard-posts of the tomb saying: 'We are hungry.' Turin Strike Papyrus, trans. P. J. Frandsen, 'Editing Reality: The Turin Strike Papyrus' (1990) What we actually have The Turin Strike Papyrus (Museo Egizio, Cat. 1880), plus thousands of ostraca from the village. How we know Translation of hieratic administrative documents; excavation of

chunks.heading: Tollund Man
chunks.text: Iron Age man with a peaceful face and a noose around his neck Tollund Man His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police. about 405 to 380 BCE Bjaeldskovdal bog, near Silkeborg, Denmark. On 8 May 1950, peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark uncovered a face so well preserved that they called the police, fearing a recent death. He had died around 405 to 380 BCE. The acidic, oxygen-poor bog had tanned his skin and preserved his head in extraordinary detail: closed eyes, short-cropped hair and a faint stubble. He wore a pointed skin cap and a belt, and around his neck was a plaited leather noose. He was about 40 and had been hanged, then laid in an old peat cutting in a curled, sleeping position. Many archaeologists interpret him as a sacrifice, although the reasons remain uncertain. A 2021 re-examination of his gut found that his last meal, eaten roughly 12 to 24 hours before death, was a porridge made mainly of barley, pale persicaria seeds and flax, with some fish. He also carried whipworm, roundworm and tapeworm. The researchers found nothing obviously festive or special about the meal. A ritual death, then, but perhaps preceded by an ordinary day's food, which makes him feel even closer to us. What we actually have A bog body whose head is exceptionally well preserved, with the noose, cap and belt; gut contents. How we know Radiocarbon dating; autopsy, X-ray and CT scanning; macrofossil, pollen, protein and parasite analysis of gut contents. At Silkeborg Museum his head is original, but most of the body on display is a replica, because only parts of it were conserved in 1950.

chunks.heading: Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai)
chunks.text: Han dynasty noblewoman with a modern-looking medical file Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai) Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach. died about 168 BCE Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan, China. In 1972, at Mawangdui near Changsha, archaeologists excavated Tomb 1, a deep Han dynasty grave sealed with thick layers of charcoal and white clay. Inside four nested coffins, in a mysterious liquid, lay Xin Zhui, wife of Li Cang, Marquis of Dai and chancellor of the Changsha kingdom. She had died around 168 BCE, at about 50, and her body was astonishingly preserved: soft skin, joints that could still bend, hair still in place. The autopsy reads like a modern medical file. She had hardened coronary arteries, gallstones, spinal problems that probably caused back pain, and schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection. In her digestive tract were more than a hundred melon seeds, suggesting she ate melon a few hours before a heart attack killed her, probably in summer. She was buried with over a thousand objects, including silk garments, lacquerware, food and a painted T-shaped silk banner that depicts a journey from the underworld to the heavens. Her body suggests the privileged life of a Han noblewoman also brought diseases we still link to rich diets and little exercise. What we actually have A remarkably preserved body, her tomb furnishings and a painted silk banner, now in the Hunan Museum, Changsha. How we know Modern medical autopsy and pathology (1972); study of tomb inscriptions and seals naming her household; later preservation research. One of the silk robes from the Mawangdui tombs is so fine that it weighs under 50 grams.

chunks.heading: The graffiti writers of Pompeii
chunks.text: A whole town of scribblers, gossips and election campaigners The graffiti writers of Pompeii Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it. up to 79 CE Pompeii, Campania, Italy. When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE it froze a town whose walls were covered in writing. Archaeologists have recorded thousands of painted notices and scratched graffiti: election endorsements, gladiator fan messages, greetings to friends, love notes, insults, sums and occasional crude boasts. One line, found in the Basilica, the Theatre and the Amphitheatre, is a joke about the whole scene: the wall deserves praise for not collapsing under so much boring writing. Graffiti were not mainly vandalism; studies of houses show messages answering one another, like comment threads. And the walls still make news. In 2018 a charcoal note in a house under renovation at the time of the eruption recorded a date equal to 17 October. The year is not written, but it supports other evidence, such as autumn fruits and lit braziers, that the eruption came later than the traditional 24 August. In January 2026, a Sorbonne-led team using reflectance transformation imaging, which lights a surface from many angles, announced 79 previously unknown graffiti in the corridor leading to the theatres, including a declaration of love and a drawing of two gladiators. Admiror, paries, te non cecidisse ruinis, qui tot scriptorum taedia sustineas. (I wonder, wall, that you have not fallen in ruins, bearing the tedious scribbles of so many writers.) CIL IV 1904, Pompeii; literal translation of the Latin What we actually have Thousands of painted and incised inscriptions catalogued in the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum volume IV, plus new finds. How we know Epigraphy (read

chunks.heading: Claudia Severa
chunks.text: Officer's wife who sent a birthday invitation on the Roman frontier Claudia Severa The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation. about 97 to 105 CE Vindolanda, Northumberland, England, UK. Around 100 CE, at the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern Britain (Hadrian's Wall came a couple of decades later), Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the commander Flavius Cerialis, received a thin wooden leaf tablet written in ink. It came from her friend Claudia Severa, wife of Aelius Brocchus, who commanded a fort nearby. The message: please come to my birthday celebration on 11 September; it will make the day more enjoyable. Most of the letter was written by a scribe. At the end, a different hand adds a personal farewell. Scholars identify this as Claudia herself, which makes these lines among the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. The tablet was excavated in 1985, one of hundreds of documents preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free layers at Vindolanda, alongside requests for beer, lists that mention socks, and a report sneering at the 'Brittunculi', the 'wretched little Britons'. What survives here is not grand history but friendship on a cold frontier: two women arranging a party, and one of them adding her own words. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail. Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, Tab. Vindol. 291, trans. A. K. Bowman and J. D. Thomas What we actually have Vindolanda tablet 291, a wooden leaf tablet written in ink, now in the British Museum (1986,1001.64). How we know Excavation of waterlogged deposits; infrared imaging of faded ink; palaeography comparing the scribe's hand with the closing hand. Another letter from Claudia to Lepidina (Tab. Vindol. 292) also survives, again with a closing i

chunks.heading: Hypatia of Alexandria
chunks.text: Mathematician, astronomer and philosopher Hypatia of Alexandria She was the most respected teacher in a great city of learning, until local politics turned lethal. died March 415 CE Alexandria, Egypt. Hypatia taught in Alexandria in the late 300s and early 400s CE, a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in a city famous for learning. Her father Theon was a mathematician who edited Euclid and wrote on Ptolemy; a heading in his commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest credits Hypatia with revising the text of one book. Later sources say she wrote commentaries on Diophantus's Arithmetica and Apollonius's Conics, though none survive clearly under her name. What survives best is her reputation. Her student Synesius, later a bishop, wrote her admiring letters, including one asking her to have a hydroscope, an instrument for weighing liquids, made for him. The church historian Socrates Scholasticus, writing a generation later, praised her learning and her public standing among the city's officials. In March 415, amid a bitter feud between the city's prefect Orestes and its bishop Cyril, a mob seized her in the street, dragged her into a church and killed her. Modern films and slogans have turned her into many symbols. The ancient sources show something more human: a brilliant teacher caught in local power struggles. made such attainments in literature and science, as to far surpass all the philosophers of her own time. Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 7.15, trans. A. C. Zenos (1890) What we actually have No body and none of her own writings securely survive; the evidence is textual: Synesius's letters to her, Socrates Scholasticus, Damascius and the Suda, and her father's commentaries. How we know Critical reading and comparison of ancient Greek sources written by he

chunks.heading: K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque
chunks.text: Maya king who ruled for 68 years K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque The inscriptions said he died at 80; his skeleton seemed to say 40; the argument took half a century to settle. 603 to 683 CE Palenque, Chiapas, Mexico. K'inich Janaab Pakal was born in 603 CE and crowned king of the Maya city of Palenque in 615, at the age of 12, after a turbulent period in which his mother, Sak K'uk', held power. He ruled for 68 years, long enough to rebuild a battered kingdom into one of the most elegant cities of the Classic Maya world. His funerary monument, the Temple of the Inscriptions, carries one of the longest Maya hieroglyphic texts. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a floor slab with holes for lifting it and found a rubble-filled staircase leading down into the pyramid. Clearing it took years. In 1952 he reached a crypt with a huge carved sarcophagus lid and a skeleton wearing a jade mosaic mask. Then came a puzzle: the inscriptions said Pakal died at 80, but the teeth suggested someone of 40 to 50. Decades of debate followed. A bioarchaeological team led by Vera Tiesler, working from 1999 to 2003, concluded the bones fit an elderly man; his soft, refined royal diet had probably spared his teeth. The texts, it seems, were right. What we actually have His skeleton, sarcophagus, jade mask and tomb in the Temple of the Inscriptions, plus hieroglyphic texts recording his life dates. How we know Decipherment of Maya hieroglyphs and calendar dates; skeletal ageing methods; bioarchaeological analysis of the tomb. His jade death mask was stolen from Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology in 1985 and recovered in 1989.

chunks.heading: The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581
chunks.text: Viking-age woman buried with a full warrior's kit The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581 For a century she was the textbook Viking warrior, assumed to be a man; then her DNA was read. mid-900s CE Birka, Bjorko island, Lake Malaren, Sweden. In the 1870s Hjalmar Stolpe excavated a chamber grave at Birka, a Viking-age trading town on an island in Lake Malaren, Sweden. Grave Bj 581, from the mid-900s, held one person buried with a sword, an axe, two spears, armour-piercing arrows, two shields, two horses and a gaming set with pieces and dice. For more than a century it served as the model of a high-status Viking warrior, assumed to be male. In 2016 the osteologist Anna Kjellstrom re-examined the skeleton and found female traits; in 2017 a genomic study found two X chromosomes and no Y. Isotopes suggest she was not born at Birka, and she was over 30 when she died. The reaction was huge, and so was the criticism. Had the bones been mixed up since the 19th century? Were the weapons gifts for someone who never fought? In 2019 the team replied, rechecking the excavation records and arguing the skeleton belongs to the grave. They left open whether she was a fighting warrior, a symbolic one or something else. The debate now centres less on her sex and more on how archaeologists read gender into grave goods for a century. What we actually have Chamber grave Bj 581 with its skeleton, weapons, horses and gaming set, documented in Stolpe's records and stored in Stockholm. How we know Osteology; ancient DNA (sex chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA); strontium isotopes for mobility; re-examination of 19th-century excavation plans. The gaming set placed on her lap has led some researchers to suggest she may have been a tactician or commander, though that remains speculative.

chunks.heading: Mansa Musa of Mali
chunks.text: Emperor whose gold made headlines in Cairo and Europe Mansa Musa of Mali He arrived in Cairo with so much gold that, according to one chronicler, the price of gold fell. ruled about 1312 to 1337 CE; journey to Cairo in 1324 Mali Empire, West Africa (recorded in Cairo, Egypt). In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca and stopped in Cairo. He came with a huge caravan and, by every account, astonishing quantities of gold. The Damascus-born official al-Umari, writing about a dozen years later using interviews with Cairo officials who had met him, reports that Musa showered gold on courtiers and office holders, and that his people spent so freely that the value of gold in Egypt fell. He also reports a court drama: told to kiss the ground before the Mamluk sultan, Musa at first refused. The visit made Mali famous far beyond Africa; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a West African king holding a gold nugget. Modern claims that Musa was the richest person who ever lived are guesses, since no figure can be calculated. And the historian Warren Schultz, checking Cairo exchange-rate records, found the gold slump real but temporary, not the twelve-year crash al-Umari describes. Even so, the episode shows West African gold at the heart of the medieval world economy. They exchanged gold until they depressed its value in Egypt and caused its price to fall. al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, trans. in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981) What we actually have Arabic chronicles (al-Umari, Ibn Khaldun, al-Maqrizi and others), Cairo exchange-rate records, and the Catalan Atlas of 1375. How we know Critical comparison of medieval Arabic sources; economic history of Mamluk coinage

chunks.heading: Pyramid Texts
chunks.text: Old Kingdom Egypt Pyramid Texts c. 2400-2300 BCE (carved); some spells likely older oral liturgy Rock solid history check. Verdict: Rock solid. Language and script Old Egyptian; hieroglyphs carved and painted on stone walls Oldest copy Walls of the burial chamber and antechamber of the Pyramid of Unas, c. 2350 BCE (Unas's reign is dated anywhere from c. 2404-2374 to c. 2312-2282 BCE) Where it is now In situ, Saqqara, Egypt Size 283 spells in Unas's pyramid alone; hundreds more across later Old Kingdom pyramids Dating confidence high for the carvings, low for oral origins What it says A launch manual for a dead king. The spells help the pharaoh climb a ladder to the sky, ride a reed float across the heavens, join the boat of the sun god Ra and become one of the stars that never set. Others are practical charms against snakes and scorpions. The notorious Cannibal Hymn has the king swallowing gods to absorb their power. It reads less like a book than a ritual toolkit, carved in stone so it would keep working forever. History check The texts sit exactly where and when they appear to belong: inside securely identified royal pyramids at Saqqara (Unas, Teti, Pepi I, Merenre, Pepi II and several queens). Their content is religious, not a chronicle, but it matches temple and tomb evidence for Old Kingdom cults of Ra and Osiris. Absolute dates for Unas still vary by several decades between chronologies. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As a record of Old Kingdom royal belief and ritual. Unas's burial chamber has a ceiling painted with golden stars. Until the 1880s, most scholars assumed pyramid interiors were blank; the carved spells were only discovered in 1880-81.

chunks.heading: Epic of Gilgamesh
chunks.text: Mesopotamia (Sumer and Babylonia) Epic of Gilgamesh Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE; Old Babylonian epic c. 1800 BCE; Standard version (attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 1200-1100 BCE Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Sumerian (early poems) and Akkadian (the epic); cuneiform on clay tablets Oldest copy Old Babylonian epic tablets (e.g. the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets); the fullest version from Nineveh, c. 1800-1700 BCE; Nineveh copies 7th c. BCE Where it is now Penn Museum, Yale Babylonian Collection; British Museum (Nineveh tablets) Size About 3,000 lines on 12 tablets in the Standard Babylonian version, with gaps still being filled Dating confidence medium What it says Gilgamesh, a bullying king of Uruk, meets his match in Enkidu, a wild man the gods create to keep him busy. They become best friends, kill the forest guardian Humbaba, snub the goddess Ishtar and slay her Bull of Heaven. The gods punish them: Enkidu dies. Terrified of death, Gilgamesh travels to Utnapishtim, survivor of a great flood, seeking immortality. He finds a plant of youth, and a snake steals it. He goes home and admires his city's walls instead. History check A Gilgamesh of Uruk appears in the Sumerian King List (with an impossible 126-year reign), and one of his legendary rivals, Enmebaragesi of Kish, is attested in his own inscriptions, so a real king around 2700 BCE is plausible. No inscription of Gilgamesh himself has been found. Uruk's huge walls are real. The flood episode borrows from the older Atrahasis story; Mesopotamian flood layers are local and of different dates. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Real city and plausibly real king; the adventures are legend. When George Smith of the British Museum read the flood tablet in 1872, he was r

chunks.heading: Enuma Elish
chunks.text: Babylonia Enuma Elish Debated, c. 1800-1100 BCE; many favour the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125-1104 BCE) Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Akkadian (Standard Babylonian); cuneiform on clay Oldest copy Tablet copies from Ashur, Kish and the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 1st millennium BCE (earliest c. 9th c. BCE) Where it is now British Museum and other collections Size About 1,100 lines on 7 tablets Dating confidence low-medium What it says Before sky and earth had names, sweet water (Apsu) and salt water (Tiamat) mingled. Their divine children are so noisy that Apsu plots to kill them; the clever god Ea strikes first. Furious, Tiamat raises an army of monsters. Young Marduk agrees to fight only if crowned king of the gods. He blasts her with winds, splits her body like a dried fish to make sky and earth, creates humans from a rebel god's blood to do the gods' chores, and builds Babylon. History check As an account of creation it is myth. As political history it fits well: it celebrates Marduk's rise to the top of the pantheon, which tracks Babylon's own rise. Later ritual texts indicate it was recited during the Akitu New Year festival. Its exact date of composition is still argued. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Mythic cosmology; reliable mirror of Babylonian politics and religion. The title just means 'When on high', the poem's first two words. The last tablet is a victory list of Marduk's 50 names.

chunks.heading: The Instruction of Ptahhotep
chunks.text: Middle Kingdom Egypt (set in the Old Kingdom) The Instruction of Ptahhotep Set in the reign of Djedkare Isesi (c. 2400 BCE); language suggests composition c. 2000-1800 BCE Plausible history check. Verdict: Plausible. Language and script Middle Egyptian; hieratic script on papyrus Oldest copy Papyrus Prisse, c. 1800 BCE (12th Dynasty) Where it is now Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris Size 37 maxims plus a prologue and epilogue Dating confidence low for the attribution, medium for Middle Kingdom composition What it says An aging vizier asks the king to let him train his son, and opens with a grumpy list of what old age does to the body. Then comes the advice: stay humble, because 'good speech is more hidden than greenstone, yet it is found among the women at the grindstones'. Listen more than you talk. Do not gossip. Do not grab food at a superior's table. Be generous, love your wife, and do not let success make you arrogant. Some tips would suit a modern office. History check King Djedkare Isesi and viziers named Ptahhotep are attested, including tombs at Saqqara. But the grammar and style point to the Middle Kingdom, so the attribution is probably a literary device giving the text an ancient pedigree. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid Real names and setting; authorship probably later than claimed. Papyrus Prisse, acquired in Egypt in the 1840s by Émile Prisse d'Avennes, is often nicknamed 'the oldest book in the world'.

chunks.heading: Code of Hammurabi
chunks.text: Old Babylonian Mesopotamia Code of Hammurabi c. 1755-1750 BCE, late in Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792-1750 BCE, middle chronology) Rock solid history check. Verdict: Rock solid. Language and script Akkadian; cuneiform carved on a basalt stele Oldest copy The 2.25 m black stone stele, c. 1754 BCE Where it is now Louvre, Paris (found at Susa, Iran, in 1901-02) Size Prologue, 282 laws (as numbered by modern scholars), epilogue Dating confidence high relative date; absolute date depends on the chronology used What it says A king announces that the gods chose him 'to make justice appear in the land' and protect the weak from the strong. Then come the case rulings: theft, trade, wages, rent, marriage, divorce, adoption, surgeons' fees and building collapses. 'An eye for an eye' applies, but only between social equals; hurting a commoner or a slave costs silver instead. If a house falls and kills its owner, the builder dies. It is justice, Bronze Age style. History check Hammurabi is one of the best-attested kings of antiquity: his letters, year names, contracts and many tablet copies of the laws survive. Scholars debate whether courts actually applied the code; few trial records cite it, so it may have worked as royal showcase and model rulings. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid The king, the text and its date are firmly attested; everyday legal use is debated. The stele was itself war loot: an Elamite king, Shutruk-Nahhunte, carried it to Susa in the 12th century BCE, and several columns were chiselled off, perhaps for a boast he never carved.

chunks.heading: Rigveda
chunks.text: Vedic Indo-Aryans, northwestern Indian subcontinent Rigveda c. 1500-1000 BCE (older hymns c. 1500-1200 BCE) Plausible history check. Verdict: Plausible. Language and script Vedic Sanskrit; transmitted orally, later written in scripts such as Sharada and Devanagari Oldest copy Manuscripts in the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute collection (UNESCO Memory of the World, 2007), Oldest dated: 1464 CE Where it is now BORI, Pune, India Size 10 books (mandalas), 1,028 hymns, about 10,600 verses Dating confidence medium; based on linguistics and external anchors What it says A collection of hymns sung at fire rituals. Agni, the fire, carries offerings to the gods. Indra, a thunder-wielding hero fuelled by the drink soma, slays the serpent Vritra and frees the rivers. Ushas, the dawn, is praised in some of its loveliest poems, and Varuna guards cosmic order. One late hymn wonders how creation began and ends with a shrug: perhaps even the highest overseer 'knows, or perhaps he does not know'. History check The hymns describe a mobile, cattle-herding society with horses and chariots, and their river names fit the Punjab region. A Hittite-Mitanni treaty of about 1380 BCE invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas, an independent sign these gods were known by the 14th century BCE. Exact dates and the question of origins remain debated. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid Reliable window on an early society; dating is approximate. The text was preserved by memory for many centuries using cross-checking recitation patterns (pada, krama, jata, ghana) that make errors easy to spot. Vedic chanting is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

chunks.heading: Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)
chunks.text: New Kingdom to Ptolemaic Egypt Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day) Emerges c. 1700-1550 BCE from earlier Coffin Texts; used until c. 50 BCE Rock solid history check. Verdict: Rock solid. Language and script Egyptian; hieroglyphic and hieratic on papyrus, coffins and shrouds Oldest copy Early spells on the coffin of Queen Mentuhotep (13th Dynasty); the famous Papyrus of Ani, c. 1700 BCE; Ani c. 1250 BCE Where it is now Coffin now lost (known from copies); Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum Size About 190 spells known; no single copy has them all. The Papyrus of Ani is over 20 m long Dating confidence high What it says A personalized survival kit for the afterlife. Spells let the dead transform into a heron or a lotus, avoid walking upside down, and keep their heart in place. The big moment is spell 125: in the Hall of Two Truths the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat while the deceased recites a 'negative confession': I have not stolen, I have not lied. Fail, and the monster Ammit, part crocodile, part lion, part hippo, eats the heart. History check Thousands of copies come from dated tombs, so the text's use and development are very well documented. It records what elite Egyptians hoped for after death rather than events. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As evidence of Egyptian funerary belief and practice. Some copies were prepared in advance with blank spaces where the buyer's name would be filled in later: a ready-made afterlife guide.

chunks.heading: Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah
chunks.text: Ancient Israel and Judah; Jewish communities of the Persian and Hellenistic eras Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah Written and edited over c. 9th/8th-2nd c. BCE; the Torah probably reached its present form c. 6th-5th c. BCE Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Biblical Hebrew with some Aramaic; Paleo-Hebrew, later Aramaic square script Oldest copy Ketef Hinnom silver amulets (the Priestly Blessing, Numbers 6:24-26); oldest complete Hebrew Bible: Leningrad Codex, Amulets c. 600 BCE; Leningrad Codex 1008 CE Where it is now Israel Museum, Jerusalem; National Library of Russia, St Petersburg Size 24 books in the Jewish count; the Torah alone is about 80,000 Hebrew words Dating confidence low-medium; actively debated What it says A library rather than a book: creation, a flood, the families of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Exodus from Egypt and laws given at Sinai, then settlement, judges, kings, prophets, exile to Babylon and return. Alongside the stories sit poetry (Psalms, Song of Songs), proverbs, the long argument of Job and the gloriously skeptical Ecclesiastes. It is history, law, poetry and argument woven together by many hands. History check Independent inscriptions confirm several figures and events: the Tel Dan stele mentions the 'House of David', the Mesha stele names Omri of Israel, Assyrian records name Jehu and Hezekiah, and Babylonian ration tablets list King Jehoiachin. The patriarchs, the Exodus and a sweeping conquest lack direct archaeological support, and the scale of the early monarchy is debated. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Later monarchy period often corroborated; earlier narratives largely untestable or unsupported. The Ketef Hinnom amulets are tiny rolled silver scrolls, found in 1979, that

chunks.heading: Iliad and Odyssey
chunks.text: Archaic Greece Iliad and Odyssey c. 750-650 BCE, from a much older oral tradition; fixed in writing between the 8th and 6th c. BCE Plausible history check. Verdict: Plausible. Language and script Homeric Greek (an artificial poetic mix of dialects); Greek alphabet Oldest copy Papyrus fragments from Egypt; oldest complete Iliad manuscript: Venetus A, Fragments from 3rd c. BCE; Venetus A 10th c. CE Where it is now Various papyrus collections; Biblioteca Marciana, Venice Size Iliad 15,693 lines; Odyssey 12,109 lines Dating confidence medium What it says The Iliad covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War: Achilles sulks after an insult, his friend Patroclus is killed, Achilles kills Hector in revenge, and old King Priam sneaks into the enemy camp to beg for his son's body. The Odyssey follows Odysseus's ten-year trip home past a Cyclops, the witch Circe, the Sirens and the land of the dead, ending with a bow contest and a hall full of doomed suitors. History check Troy is identified with Hisarlik in Turkey, a real city destroyed more than once around 1300-1180 BCE. Hittite texts mention Wilusa (likely Ilios), a king called Alaksandu and a western power called Ahhiyawa (likely Achaeans). The boar's-tusk helmet in the Iliad matches Mycenaean finds. The heroes, gods and a single ten-year war remain unattested. History check Plausible Busted Rock solid A real Bronze Age setting with a possible kernel of conflict, heavily legendary. There is no Trojan Horse in the Iliad. It appears only as a memory in the Odyssey (books 4 and 8), and the full tale is told much later by Virgil.

chunks.heading: Avesta
chunks.text: Ancient Iranian peoples; Zoroastrian tradition Avesta Gathas perhaps c. 1500-1000 BCE (proposals range to c. 500 BCE); Young Avestan texts later; written down in Sasanian times Hot debate history check. Verdict: Hot debate. Language and script Avestan (Old and Young Avestan); written in the Avestan alphabet, invented c. 5th-6th c. CE Oldest copy Manuscripts J2 and L4, the oldest securely dated, 1323 CE Where it is now UK libraries (Oxford and London); over 300 Avestan manuscripts are known Size About 83,000 surviving words, perhaps a quarter of the Sasanian-era Avesta Dating confidence low What it says At its heart are the Gathas, 17 hymns attributed to the prophet Zarathustra, who talks directly with the wise lord Ahura Mazda. The big theme is choice: every person sides with truth (asha) or with the lie (druj). Around the Gathas sit liturgies for the fire ritual, hymns to divine beings such as Mithra and Anahita, and the Vendidad, a rulebook on purity, dogs, and how to keep the dead from polluting earth, fire and water. History check The Gathas' language is very close to Rigvedic Sanskrit, which supports an early date. Achaemenid inscriptions of Darius I (c. 520 BCE) invoke Ahuramazda, so the god was central by then. Zarathustra himself has no external attestation, and his date is one of the most contested in the history of religion. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid The tradition is ancient; the founder's date and life are uncertain. The Avestan alphabet, with more than 50 letters, was invented centuries after the texts were composed, largely to record pronunciation precisely as priests chanted it.

chunks.heading: Shijing (Classic of Poetry)
chunks.text: Zhou dynasty China Shijing (Classic of Poetry) c. 1000-600 BCE Strong history check. Verdict: Strong. Language and script Old Chinese; Chinese characters on bamboo and silk Oldest copy Warring States bamboo slips held by Anhui University; Han-era Fuyang slips, c. 4th c. BCE; Fuyang c. 165 BCE Where it is now Anhui University, Hefei; Fuyang material in Anhui Size 305 poems Dating confidence medium-high What it says China's oldest poetry anthology. The 'Airs of the States' are folk songs about love, flirting by the river, harvests, homesick soldiers and brides leaving home. One poem begs a 'big rat' to stop eating the grain: a thinly veiled complaint about greedy lords. The court odes and temple hymns praise Zhou ancestors such as King Wen and King Wu, who overthrew the Shang. It is sung history and everyday feeling in one. History check Kings and events named in the hymns match Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, including the Zhou conquest of the Shang (c. 1046 BCE). Bamboo manuscripts from the 4th century BCE show the poems circulated before the Qin book burning, with variant wording. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Names and institutions largely match bronze-age inscriptions. Tradition says Confucius picked these 305 from about 3,000 poems; most scholars doubt it. He did tell his son that without studying the Odes, 'you will have nothing to say'.

chunks.heading: Analects of Confucius (Lunyu)
chunks.text: Lu state, Spring and Autumn to Han China Analects of Confucius (Lunyu) Compiled by disciples and later followers, c. 5th-3rd c. BCE, taking final shape by the Han Strong history check. Verdict: Strong. Language and script Classical Chinese; Chinese characters on bamboo slips Oldest copy Dingzhou bamboo slips; Haihun marquis tomb slips, Before 55 BCE (Dingzhou) and 59 BCE (Haihun) Where it is now Hebei and Jiangxi provinces, China Size 20 books, about 500 short passages, roughly 16,000 characters Dating confidence medium What it says Short sayings and scenes starring a teacher and his students. 'Is it not a pleasure to learn and practice what you have learned?' opens the book. Confucius praises humaneness (ren), ritual (li) and the gentleman who does not impose on others what he would not want himself. He can be funny and exasperated too: catching a student napping in the daytime, he says rotten wood cannot be carved. History check Confucius (traditionally 551-479 BCE) is widely accepted as historical, and other early texts mention him and his disciples. But the Analects was assembled in layers over generations, so individual sayings are hard to pin on him directly. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Historical teacher; the exact words are layered. The tomb of Liu He, Marquis of Haihun (d. 59 BCE), yielded slips that may belong to the lost 'Qi' version of the Analects, including a chapter title unseen for nearly 2,000 years.

chunks.heading: Tao Te Ching (Daodejing)
chunks.text: Warring States China Tao Te Ching (Daodejing) c. 4th c. BCE (with older sayings); traditionally attributed to Laozi, 6th c. BCE Hot debate history check. Verdict: Hot debate. Language and script Classical Chinese; bamboo slips and silk Oldest copy Guodian bamboo slips (partial); Mawangdui silk manuscripts (complete), c. 300 BCE; c. 168 BCE Where it is now Hubei Provincial Museum; Hunan Museum Size About 5,000 characters in 81 short chapters Dating confidence low for author, medium for dating What it says A tiny book of big paradoxes. 'The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.' Water is soft yet wears down stone, so yielding beats forcing. The wise ruler practises wu wei, acting without straining, and governs a great state 'like cooking a small fish': do not poke it too much. It praises simplicity, humility and knowing when enough is enough, and it makes fun of cleverness and showy virtue. History check Laozi's biography comes from Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE), who himself offered several candidates. The Guodian slips show that sections of the text existed by about 300 BCE, but not necessarily as one book by one author. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid The text is ancient; its author may be legendary. The Mawangdui silk copies put the 'Te' half first, so the oldest complete versions are really the Te Tao Ching.

chunks.heading: Pali Canon (Tipitaka)
chunks.text: Theravada Buddhist tradition, South and Southeast Asia Pali Canon (Tipitaka) Oral teachings from c. 5th c. BCE; written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st c. BCE Strong history check. Verdict: Strong. Language and script Pali; written in Sinhala, Burmese, Khmer, Thai, Pyu and later Roman scripts Oldest copy The Pyu 'golden Pali text': 20 gold leaves, c. 5th-6th c. CE Where it is now Found at Sri Ksetra, Myanmar Size Three 'baskets' (discipline, discourses, higher teaching); dozens of volumes in printed editions Dating confidence medium What it says The Vinaya sets rules for monks and nuns, and often explains each rule with the story of the monk whose mishap caused it. The Suttas hold the Buddha's talks: the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, and parables like the raft you leave behind once you have crossed the river, or blind men arguing over what an elephant is. The Abhidhamma breaks the mind into moments and parts like an early psychology manual. History check Ashoka's inscriptions (3rd c. BCE) mention the Buddha, and the Lumbini pillar states that the Buddha was born there. The Buddha's own dates remain debated (c. 563-483 or c. 480-400 BCE). The oldest Buddhist manuscripts of all are Gandharan birch-bark scrolls in the Gandhari language, not Pali. History check Strong Busted Rock solid Historical teacher and early community; wording shaped by centuries of oral transmission. Sri Lankan chronicles say monks wrote the canon down at Aluvihare cave after famine and war threatened the people who held it in memory.

chunks.heading: Mahabharata
chunks.text: Ancient India Mahabharata c. 400 BCE-400 CE, in layers Hot debate history check. Verdict: Hot debate. Language and script Sanskrit; transmitted orally and in many scripts Oldest copy Spitzer Manuscript fragment listing the epic's books; complete manuscripts much later, Spitzer c. 2nd c. CE; full manuscripts from the 2nd millennium CE Where it is now Spitzer fragments from Kizil, Xinjiang; full manuscripts in Indian and Nepalese collections Size About 100,000 couplets in the traditional count; roughly seven times the Iliad and Odyssey combined by lines Dating confidence medium What it says A family feud that becomes a world war. The five Pandava brothers lose their kingdom and their shared wife Draupadi's dignity in a rigged dice game, survive 13 years of exile, then face their cousins the Kauravas in an 18-day battle at Kurukshetra. Just before the fighting, Krishna counsels the hesitant archer Arjuna: that dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita. The epic claims, with some justification, that what is here is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere. History check The Kuru kingdom was real (Iron Age, c. 1200-500 BCE, associated with Painted Grey Ware culture), and excavations at Hastinapura found a settlement of that period. No archaeological trace of a great war has been found, and astronomical dates proposed for it (such as 3102 BCE) are disputed. History check Hot debate Busted Rock solid Real Iron Age polity; the war and heroes are unverified. In the frame story the sage Vyasa dictates the epic to the elephant-headed god Ganesha, who agrees to write only if Vyasa never pauses, and breaks off a tusk to use as a pen.

chunks.heading: Histories of Herodotus
chunks.text: Classical Greece (Herodotus of Halicarnassus) Histories of Herodotus c. 440-425 BCE Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Ionic Greek; Greek alphabet Oldest copy Papyrus fragments from Oxyrhynchus; oldest complete manuscript Codex Laurentianus 70.3, Fragments 1st-3rd c. CE; codex 10th c. CE Where it is now Oxford and other papyrus collections; Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence Size 9 books; roughly 190,000 Greek words Dating confidence high What it says The first big 'inquiry' (historia) in Greek: why did Greeks and Persians go to war? Along the way Herodotus detours into everything. Egyptian crocodiles and mummification, Scythian steam baths, a singer rescued by a dolphin, King Croesus misreading an oracle, and Indian ants that dig up gold. Then the main event: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis, told with a sharp eye for pride and its fall. History check Persian royal inscriptions and the Persepolis administrative tablets confirm many names and institutions; the Behistun inscription parallels his account of Darius's rise. Frozen Scythian tombs match some of the customs he describes. Some numbers are inflated, notably Xerxes' army of millions, and some stories are hearsay he admits he doubts. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Core events and many details corroborated; numbers and tall tales are not. Explorer Michel Peissel proposed that the gold-digging 'ants' were Himalayan marmots, whose burrows on one high plateau throw up gold dust.

chunks.heading: New Testament
chunks.text: Early Christian communities, eastern Roman Empire New Testament c. 50-120 CE (Paul's letters c. 50-60; Gospels c. 70-100) Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Koine Greek; Greek uncial script on papyrus and parchment Oldest copy Papyrus P52 (a few verses of John 18); oldest complete New Testament: Codex Sinaiticus, P52 c. 125-175 CE (dating debated); Sinaiticus mid-4th c. CE Where it is now John Rylands Library, Manchester; mostly British Library, London Size 27 books; about 138,000 Greek words Dating confidence medium-high What it says Four Gospels tell the life, teaching, death and reported resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth from different angles. Acts follows the early movement from Jerusalem to Rome. Then come letters, many by Paul, full of advice, theology and arguments with local congregations, and finally Revelation, a vivid apocalyptic vision packed with symbolic beasts and numbers. Its most famous passages, from the Sermon on the Mount to the parable of the Good Samaritan, still shape everyday language. History check Most historians accept that Jesus existed and was executed under Pontius Pilate; Tacitus and Josephus mention him. A 1961 inscription from Caesarea names Pilate as prefect of Judea. Some details are problematic, such as the census of Quirinius (6 CE) versus Herod's death (4 BCE). Miracle claims lie outside what historical method can test. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Setting and several figures corroborated; many events untestable. P52 is about the size of a credit card. More than 5,000 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament survive, more than for any other ancient text.

chunks.heading: Popol Vuh
chunks.text: K'iche' Maya, highland Guatemala Popol Vuh Written c. 1554-1558 CE from much older traditions Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script K'iche' Mayan written in the Latin alphabet Oldest copy Francisco Ximénez's manuscript, K'iche' and Spanish in parallel columns, c. 1701-1703 CE Where it is now Newberry Library, Chicago Size Four parts; roughly 8,000-9,000 lines in line-by-line translations Dating confidence high for the writing; older sources uncertain What it says The gods try to make people who will praise them. Mud people melt. Wooden people have no hearts, so their own dogs, pots and grinding stones rise up against them. Before humans are made from maize, the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque play the ballgame against the lords of the underworld, Xibalba, survive the House of Razors and the House of Bats, outwit death, and rise as the sun and moon. Then comes the history of K'iche' lineages. History check Scenes of the Hero Twins and the maize god appear in Classic Maya art, and related maize-god imagery appears in the San Bartolo murals of about 100 BCE, showing these myths are far older than the manuscript. The later dynastic sections match other K'iche' documents and the ruins of their capital, Q'umarkaj. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Myths are ancient and corroborated in art; late dynastic history reasonably supported. The original K'iche' manuscript is lost. The text survived only because a Dominican friar copied it around 1701; the copy resurfaced in Guatemala in the 1850s and now sits in Chicago.

chunks.heading: Quran
chunks.text: 7th-century Arabia Quran 610-632 CE (traditional period of revelation); compiled as a standard codex c. 650 CE by tradition Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Classical Arabic; early Hijazi script, later Kufic Oldest copy The Birmingham leaves (two parchment folios); other early witnesses include the Sanaa palimpsest, Parchment radiocarbon-dated to 568-645 CE (95% probability) Where it is now Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham (Mingana Collection) Size 114 suras, 6,236 verses (common count), about 77,000 words Dating confidence high for an early date, supported by manuscript evidence What it says Arabic scripture presented as recited revelation. Its themes include one God, gratitude, justice, care for orphans and the poor, and a coming day of judgement. It retells stories of figures shared with Jewish and Christian traditions, such as Abraham, Moses, Mary and Jesus, often briefly and with a moral point, and it gives guidance on law and community life. It is famous for rhythmic rhymed prose meant to be heard aloud. History check Radiocarbon dates on early parchments (Birmingham, Tubingen, Sanaa) support a written text very early, consistent with a 7th-century origin. Its references to ancient figures overlap with biblical traditions and are largely beyond archaeological testing, as with other scriptures. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Early textual history well supported; ancient narratives largely untestable. The Birmingham leaves sat in a university collection for about 90 years before a researcher's close look led to radiocarbon testing in 2015.

chunks.heading: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters)
chunks.text: Nara-period Japan Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters) Presented to the court in 712 CE Mixed record history check. Verdict: Mixed record. Language and script Old Japanese written with Chinese characters, partly as Chinese prose and partly phonetically Oldest copy Shinpukuji manuscript, copied by the monk Ken'yu (a National Treasure), 1371-1372 CE Where it is now Shinpukuji temple (Osu Kannon), Nagoya Size 3 volumes Dating confidence high What it says Two gods, Izanagi and Izanami, stir the ocean with a jeweled spear, and the drips form the islands of Japan. Izanami dies giving birth to fire, and Izanagi follows her to the land of the dead, then flees in horror. The sun goddess Amaterasu hides in a cave and darkens the world until the gods throw a raucous party outside. Her brother Susanoo slays an eight-headed serpent and finds a sword in its tail. Then come the emperors. History check The first emperor Jimmu's traditional date (660 BCE) is not supported by archaeology, which shows the Yayoi and Kofun periods instead. Later reigns fit better: a 5th-century sword inscription from Inariyama names a king widely matched to Emperor Yuryaku. Chinese records mention a queen Himiko who does not appear in the Kojiki at all. History check Mixed record Busted Rock solid Mythic early chapters; later royal history partly corroborated. The compiler, O no Yasumaro, wrote down what the court reciter Hieda no Are had memorized. Yasumaro's own tomb and bronze epitaph were found in 1979 in a Nara tea field.

chunks.heading: Dead Sea Scrolls
chunks.text: Second Temple Judea Dead Sea Scrolls Copied c. 250 BCE-68 CE Rock solid history check. Verdict: Rock solid. Language and script Hebrew, Aramaic and some Greek; mostly square Jewish script, some Paleo-Hebrew Oldest copy The scrolls are themselves the old copies; the Great Isaiah Scroll is the showpiece, Oldest fragments 3rd c. BCE; Great Isaiah Scroll c. 2nd c. BCE Where it is now Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and other collections Size About 900-1,000 manuscripts in tens of thousands of fragments from 11 caves near Qumran (found 1947-1956) Dating confidence high (handwriting study plus radiocarbon) What it says A library hidden in desert caves. It holds the oldest known copies of almost every book of the Hebrew Bible (Esther is missing), plus writings no one had seen for 2,000 years: rules for a strict community, a War Scroll about the 'Sons of Light' fighting the 'Sons of Darkness', hymns, calendars, commentaries, and the Copper Scroll, a list of hidden treasure engraved on metal. History check Radiocarbon tests and handwriting analysis agree on dates from about the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE; the nearby Qumran settlement was destroyed around 68 CE. The Isaiah scroll is remarkably close to the medieval text, while other books show variant versions, showing both careful copying and a still-fluid text. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid As direct evidence of how scriptures were copied and read in the Second Temple period. The first scrolls were found in 1946-47 by Bedouin shepherds, reportedly while looking for a stray goat. The Copper Scroll lists dozens of treasure caches; none has ever been found.

chunks.heading: Rosetta Stone
chunks.text: Ptolemaic Egypt Rosetta Stone 196 BCE (decree of priests at Memphis honouring Ptolemy V) Rock solid history check. Verdict: Rock solid. Language and script Egyptian in hieroglyphic and Demotic scripts, plus Ancient Greek Oldest copy The granodiorite stele itself, about 760 kg, 196 BCE; found July 1799 at Rashid (Rosetta) Where it is now British Museum, London (since 1802) Size 14 surviving lines of hieroglyphs, 32 of Demotic, 54 of Greek Dating confidence high What it says Surprisingly, a piece of bureaucracy. Priests thank the young king Ptolemy V for tax breaks, gifts to temples and crushing a rebellion, and in return vote him statues and festivals. The key line orders the decree to be set up in every major temple in 'sacred', 'native' and Greek writing. That last detail made it the key: one message in three scripts, one of which scholars could already read. History check Other copies of the same decree have been found, and its events match the known reign of Ptolemy V. Using the Greek as a guide, Thomas Young made early progress and Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822. History check Rock solid Busted Rock solid An official dated document; its account of a royal decree is corroborated. Legend says Champollion ran into his brother's office shouting 'Je tiens l'affaire!' ('I've got it!') and then fainted.

chunks.heading: The Great Pyramid of Khufu
chunks.text: Giza plateau, west bank of the Nile, Egypt The Great Pyramid of Khufu c. 2560 BCE (4th Dynasty, reign of Khufu, c. 2589-2566 BCE) Mystery. c. 146.6 m (now c. 138.5 m) Original height c. 230.3 m Base side c. 2.3 million (estimate, not a count) Estimated blocks c. 6 million tonnes Estimated mass c. 40 boatmen; about 2-3 round trips every 10 days, c. 30 blocks of 2-3 t per trip Merer's crew c. 64 km long, 200-700 m wide, bordering 31 pyramids Ahramat Nile branch at least 30 m long, above the Grand Gallery Big Void (2017) c. 9 m long, c. 2 x 2 m section, c. 20 m above ground North Face Corridor (2023) How it was made The strongest evidence comes from the builders' own paperwork. Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt's oldest known harbour, include the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew of about 40 men shipped white Tura limestone to Giza in Khufu's 27th year, using canals and a harbour basin. A 2024 study used radar satellite imagery, geophysics and sediment cores to map a buried Nile branch, the Ahramat, running past 31 pyramids, which suggests water transport reached close to the building sites. Most core blocks were quarried on the plateau itself. Ramps, sledges and water-wetted sand are well attested, though the exact ramp layout used for the upper courses remains debated. The myth The pyramid is too precise to have been built with Bronze Age tools, and the 2025 radar 'discovery' of giant shafts and chambers hundreds of metres beneath the neighbouring Khafre pyramid reveals a hidden lost-civilisation complex. The reality Quarries, tool marks, workers' settlements and cemeteries, bakeries, and Merer's logbook document an organised Egyptian workforce. chunks.heading: Gobekli Tepe
chunks.text: Germus mountains near Sanliurfa, southeastern Turkey Gobekli Tepe c. 9500-8000 BCE (Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B) Mystery. about 11,500 years (roughly 6,000 years older than Stonehenge's sarsen circle) Age c. 5.5 m (central pillars of Enclosure D) Tallest pillars c. 10 tonnes Heaviest pillars c. 300 m across, c. 15 m high (c. 9 ha) Mound 4 main ones (A-D); more detected by geophysics Big enclosures excavated none: built before both Pottery or metal How it was made Hunter-gatherers, and possibly early cultivators, quarried T-shaped limestone pillars from the plateau around the site using flint tools; unfinished pillars still lie in the quarries, one about 7 m long. The pillars were set into rock-cut sockets or low benches inside round-to-oval stone walls. Geometric analysis by Haklay and Gopher (2020) suggests the three main enclosures were laid out together around an equilateral triangle, implying an overall plan. Carved foxes, boars, snakes and vultures, plus human arms and belts on the pillars, point to stylised figures. Evidence of large-scale grain processing and beer-like brewing suggests feasting drew labour together, and recent excavation shows houses, cisterns and daily life on site. The myth Gobekli Tepe is a temple of a lost advanced civilisation, deliberately buried to hide it, with a star map encoding an ancient comet catastrophe. The reality Everything found (flint tools, animal bones, grinding stones, burials of domestic life) fits a Neolithic community. Current excavators interpret the fill as slope slides and gradual debris build-up rather than one deliberate burial, and see a settlement with monumental buildings rather than an isolated temple. chunks.heading: Stonehenge
chunks.text: Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, England Stonehenge c. 3000-1500 BCE; sarsen circle and trilithons c. 2500 BCE Mystery. up to c. 25-30 tonnes; c. 7 m tall trilithon uprights Largest sarsens West Woods, c. 25 km north (most of the 52 tested) Sarsen source Preseli Hills, Wales, c. 225 km Bluestone source c. 6 tonnes, c. 4.9 m long, sandstone Altar Stone Orcadian Basin, NE Scotland, c. 700 km away Altar Stone origin aligned on midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset Solstice axis How it was made Stonehenge grew in stages over about 1,500 years. An earthwork enclosure came first around 3000 BCE; the great sarsen circle and trilithons followed around 2500 BCE. Geochemistry matched most sarsens to West Woods, about 25 km away, and the bluestones to specific outcrops in the Preseli Hills of Wales. In 2024, the age of zircon and rutile grains showed the 6-tonne Altar Stone came from the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland; a 2025-2026 follow-up found no realistic glacial route, so people most likely moved it, by land, sea or both. The stones were shaped with stone hammers, and joined with woodworking joints: mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove. The myth The stones are too heavy and far-travelled for Neolithic farmers, so they must have been moved by magic (Merlin in medieval legend) or dropped nearby by glaciers. The reality Quarry sites with stone wedges and tools have been identified in Preseli, and Neolithic groups had sledges, rollers, ropes and boats. Experimental archaeology has moved multi-tonne stones with teams of a few dozen people. The mineral fingerprinting of the Altar Stone and ice-sheet modelling point to deliberate human transport over hundreds of kilometres, which says something remarkable about connections across Neolithic Britain. chunks.text: Recovered from a shipwreck off Antikythera, Greece The Antikythera Mechanism Made c. 2nd-1st century BCE; wreck c. 70-60 BCE; found 1901 Mystery. 82 Surviving fragments 30 (bronze, hand-cut triangular teeth) Surviving gears roughly shoebox size, c. 34 x 18 x 9 cm (reconstruction) Original case most likely 354 holes (lunar year), radius c. 77.1 mm (2024 analysis) Calendar ring average radial variation c. 0.028 mm Hole placement precision Metonic 19-year, Saros 18-year eclipse cycle, Olympiad games cycle, planets (reconstructed) Cycles modelled How it was made The device was a hand-cranked bronze gear train in a wooden case. X-ray computed tomography (2005 onward) read hidden gear-tooth counts and thousands of characters of inscribed instructions. Those tooth counts match Babylonian and Greek astronomical cycles: the Metonic cycle, the Saros eclipse cycle, and a pin-and-slot gear that models the Moon's changing speed. Freeth and colleagues (2021) reconstructed a front display of the known planets based on inscribed period relations. Gears were cut by hand from bronze sheet, with triangular teeth. A 2024 statistical study of the surviving calendar ring suggests 354 holes, matching a lunar calendar, and shows the maker placed them with sub-millimetre care. The myth Nothing like it existed for 1,400 years, so it must be out-of-place technology, perhaps from visitors or a vanished super-civilisation. The reality It sits within a documented Greek tradition: Cicero describes geared spheres attributed to Archimedes and Posidonius, and the inscriptions use Greek astronomical language and Babylonian-derived cycle data. chunks.heading: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World (and the Hanging Gardens puzzle)
chunks.text: Eastern Mediterranean and Mesopotamia The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World (and the Hanging Gardens puzzle) List canonised c. 2nd century BCE (Antipater of Sidon, Philo of Byzantium); monuments c. 2560-280 BCE Mystery. 1 of 7 (the Great Pyramid) Wonders still standing about 2,300 years apart (Great Pyramid c. 2560 BCE; Lighthouse of Alexandria c. 280 BCE) Oldest to newest Colossus of Rhodes, c. 33 m tall, stood c. 54-56 years before an earthquake c. 226 BCE Shortest-lived 0 known Babylonian texts mentioning the Gardens written centuries after Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605-562 BCE) Earliest surviving Greek descriptions Sennacherib's palace garden at Nineveh, c. 700 BCE Dalley's candidate How it was made The list itself was built by Greek writers: it was a travel canon of 'theamata' (things to be seen), not an official ranking, and its membership changed until settling in Roman and later times. Each wonder used distinct methods: cut-stone mass (Pyramid), bronze plates over an iron and stone frame (Colossus), marble architecture (Mausoleum, Temple of Artemis). For the Hanging Gardens, Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley argues the classical accounts describe Sennacherib's terraced garden at Nineveh, watered by a canal network including the stone aqueduct at Jerwan. Sennacherib's own inscriptions boast of casting large bronze water-raising devices, which Dalley reads as early screw pumps. The myth The Hanging Gardens were a real, precisely located Babylonian marvel built by Nebuchadnezzar II for a homesick queen; or, alternatively, the whole list is just legend. The reality Six wonders are well attested by ruins, coins or reliable descriptions.
